title: The Community Rule (1QS), translated by G. Vermes, col. III: the two spirits
authors: Vermes, G. (translator)
venue: CCAT, University of Pennsylvania (course text, R. Kraft)
ask_addressed: Read and quote the Dead Sea Scrolls themselves from open translations or scholarly pages (Community Rule, War Scroll, Damascus Document, Pesher Habakkuk, Temple Scroll, Copper Scroll, Great Isaiah Scroll and Cave 4 biblical manuscripts as witnesses to the Hebrew Bible)
quote: by the Prince of Light and walk in the ways of light, but all the children of falsehood are ruled
summary: Treatise on the Two Spirits as Vermes translates it: God appoints two spirits, truth and falsehood; the children of righteousness are ruled by the Prince of Light, the children of falsehood by the Angel of Darkness. The page is a translation only, with no apparatus or Hebrew.
limits: Translation date not printed on the page. Composition range is a judgement from two pages I opened: Iranica says the sect was founded in the mid-2nd c. BCE; Jull et al. Appendix 1 gives the 1QS col. XI hand as c. 100-75 BCE (Cross). Hempel's abstract shows the Treatise's place in the Rule is debated. Says nothing on who wrote it.

text.edition: G. Vermes translation as posted on CCAT (Penn), course file '1QS'

composition.basis: Uncertain. Sect founded mid-2nd c. BCE per Duchesne-Guillemin (Encyclopaedia Iranica); 1QS col. XI hand c. 100-75 BCE (Cross, quoted in Jull et al. 1995, App. 1). The Treatise may be older than the Rule (debated).

text.witness: 1QS from Cave 1, hand c. 100-75 BCE (Cross, in Jull et al. 1995 App. 1); 4Q258 (Cave 4 copy) script 'beginning of the first century BCE' (Cross, in Jull et al.). 1QS itself was not radiocarbon-dated in Jull et al.; 4Q258 was.

title: Damascus Document (CD), Schechter 1910 base text: the Teacher of Righteousness

quote: to make them walk in the way of His heart.
summary: The Genizah text of CD 1 says that after twenty years of groping God raised a 'teacher of righteousness' for the repentant remnant. This is the Teacher's first appearance in the Damascus Document.
limits: Page is Schechter's 1910 translation of the medieval Genizah copies; the Qumran Cave 4 copies (4Q266 etc.) are the ancient witnesses. The passage gives no name or date; the Teacher's date is inferred from other texts (Collins: first half of the 1st c. BCE, per the ASOR blog; Rodley and Thiering argue later).

text.edition: Schechter 1910 translation as posted on CCAT (Penn)

composition.basis: Best-effort window from the Cave 4 copy: 4Q266 is in a Hasmonean semi-cursive hand, '100-50 BC' (Baumgarten; Stegemann 75-50 BC), listed in Jull et al. 1995 App. 1. That dates a copy, not composition, which is earlier or contemporary.

text.witness: Cairo Genizah MSS A and B (named on the page; no date read there); Qumran 4Q266 hand 100-50 BCE, radiocarbon-dated in Jull et al. 1995 (DSS-1).

title: Commentary on Habakkuk (1QpHab), translated by G. Vermes, rev. R. A. Kraft: Teacher of Righteousness and Wicked Priest
authors: Vermes, G.; Kraft, R. A.

summary: 1QpHab (on Hab 2:2) says God made known to the Teacher of Righteousness all the mysteries of the prophets' words; col. 8 accuses the Wicked Priest, who 'forsook God and betrayed the precepts for the sake of riches'. Both are coded titles, not names.
limits: The page does not identify the figures. Composition date is contested: Rodley and Thiering (Radiocarbon 41, 1999) argue a 1st c. CE setting for the Kittim; Collins puts the Teacher in the first half of the 1st c. BCE (ASOR blog). Translation date not printed.

text.locator: col. VII 4-5 (Teacher); col. VIII 8-13 (Wicked Priest, on Hab 2:5-6)
text.language: Hebrew, quoted in English (Vermes, revised Kraft)
text.edition: Vermes translation, revised R. A. Kraft, CCAT (Penn)

composition.basis: Disputed; no window fixed here. The copy is early Herodian, c. 30-1 BCE (Cross/Avigad, in Jull et al. 1995 App. 1), so composition is at or before that on the mainstream view; Rodley and Thiering 1999 argue for a 1st c. CE setting.

text.witness: 1QpHab (Cave 1), hand c. 30-1 BCE (Jull et al. App. 1); radiocarbon on this scroll (DSS-3) in Jull et al. 1995 Table 2, 14C age 2054 +/- 22 BP.

authors: Meade, J.

quote: He will see light and be satisfied
summary: The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaa) reads 'he will see light and be satisfied' at Isa 53:11, where the Masoretic Text has no 'light'; the post lists 1QIsab, 4QIsad and the Septuagint as agreeing and argues the longer reading is original.

title: Radiocarbon Dating of Scrolls and Linen Fragments from the Judean Desert
authors: Jull, A. J. T.; Donahue, D. J.; Broshi, M.; Tov, E.
ask_addressed: Give the discovery (1946-47, Cave 1) and the dating evidence: radiocarbon (Jull et al. 1995, Radiocarbon 37; Bonani 1992), palaeography, and the competing readings of who wrote them (Essene hypothesis vs Golb's Jerusalem-library theory vs others)
quote: The radiocarbon results are in good agreement with estimates of age based on paleography.
summary: AMS dates on 18 texts and 2 linen pieces (Arizona) fit the palaeographic dates except the first sample of 4Q258; 1QIsaa at 2141 +/- 32 BP agrees with the earlier Zurich value. Two documentary texts, 4Q342 and 4Q344, are dated as late as Bar-Kokhba and thought mixed in by dealers (Broshi).
limits: Measures the age of parchment, not of composition. Calibration and sample-cleaning issues (castor oil on some parchments) are raised in Rodley and Thiering 1999, which discusses Doudna's 1998 reanalysis. Authors are affiliated with the Israel Museum Shrine of the Book (Broshi) and the Dead Sea Scrolls Publication Project (Tov), which supplied the samples; no conflict statement on the page.

title: Radiocarbon Dating of Fourteen Dead Sea Scrolls
authors: Bonani, G.; Ivy, S.; Wolfli, W.; Broshi, M.; Carmi, I.; Strugnell, J.
venue: Radiocarbon 34(3): 843-849 (Proceedings of the 14th International Radiocarbon Conference)
ask_addressed: Give the discovery (1946-47, Cave 1) and the dating evidence: radiocarbon (Jull et al. 1995, Radiocarbon 37; Bonani 1992), palaeography, and the competing readings of who wrote them (Essene hypothesis vs Golb's Jerusalem-library theory vs others)
quote: The calibrated radiocarbon ages agree well, except in one case, with the paleographic estimates or the specific dates noted on the scrolls.
summary: The Zurich AMS study of 14 selected scrolls checked palaeographic dating: ages matched the palaeographic or stated dates in all but one case. Only the abstract page was open (full PDF behind Cambridge access).
limits: Only the abstract was read, so per-scroll results are not given here. Rodley (1993) argues the conventional ages run about 40 years too old. Co-authors include M. Broshi (Israel Museum) and J. Strugnell (Harvard Divinity School); no stake statement on the abstract page.

title: An Assessment of the Radiocarbon Dating of the Dead Sea Scrolls
authors: Rodley, G. A.

quote: are offset systematically by about +40 yr
summary: A statistical reanalysis of the Zurich results: the conventional ages look about 40 years too old, and a correction gives closer agreement with palaeographic and dated texts, so 14C may be more precise than first thought.
limits: Abstract only (full PDF behind Cambridge access); a note, not a new measurement; it challenges the raw ages while broadly backing the palaeographic dates.

title: Use of Radiocarbon Dating in Assessing Christian Connections to the Dead Sea Scrolls
authors: Rodley, G. A.; Thiering, B. E.
ask_addressed: Give the discovery (1946-47, Cave 1) and the dating evidence: radiocarbon (Jull et al. 1995, Radiocarbon 37; Bonani 1992), palaeography, and the competing readings of who wrote them (Essene hypothesis vs Golb's Jerusalem-library theory vs others)

title: The Origins of the Dead Sea Scrolls (adapted from Who Wrote the Dead Sea Scrolls? 1995)
authors: Golb, N.
venue: Fathom Archive, University of Chicago (excerpt of Scribner 1995)
ask_addressed: Give the discovery (1946-47, Cave 1) and the dating evidence: radiocarbon (Jull et al. 1995, Radiocarbon 37; Bonani 1992), palaeography, and the competing readings of who wrote them (Essene hypothesis vs Golb's Jerusalem-library theory vs others)
quote: Taken from Jerusalem libraries and personal collections at a crucial hour and hidden away in many places in the wilderness
summary: Golb's thesis in his own words: the Scrolls are remains of Jerusalem libraries and private collections hidden in the Judaean Wilderness before 70 CE, not a sectarian library; he also says the 'Qumran-Essene hypothesis had become a fact in the minds of the editors' and points to over fifty hands in Cave 1.
limits: Advocacy by the proponent; the excerpt gives the manuscript argument but not the archaeological case for a fortress. Many scholars still accept an Essene or yahad link (Virtual Qumran; Collins in the ASOR blog), and the Temple-library idea does not by itself explain the sectarian texts (Virtual Qumran).
